claim: Human somatic cells may contain up to seven histone H1 variants (H1.1 to H1.5, H1.0, and H1X).
source: Human somatic cells may contain up to seven H1 variants (H1.1 to H1.5, H1.0, and H1X).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction as established knowledge about H1 variant composition in human cells.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 are universally enriched at the nuclear periphery in all cell lines analyzed.
source: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 are universally enriched at the nuclear periphery in all cell lines analyzed and co-localize with compacted DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data across multiple cell lines shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: H1X is universally enriched in high-GC regions and abundant in the nucleoli.
source: H1.4 and H1X are distributed throughout the nucleus, being H1X universally enriched in high-GC regions and abundant in the nucleoli.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figures 1, 3, and 5.

claim: H1.4 and H1.0 show a more peripheral distribution in cell lines lacking H1.3 and H1.5.
source: Interestingly, H1.4 and H1.0 show a more peripheral distribution in cell lines lacking H1.3 and H1.5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: H1X shows a distinct response to the inhibition of ribosomal DNA transcription compared to phosphorylated H1.4.
source: The differential distribution patterns of H1 suggest specific functionalities in organizing lamina-associated domains or nucleolar activity, which is further supported by a distinct response of H1X or phosphorylated H1.4 to the inhibition of ribosomal DNA transcription.
evidence: This is supported by ActD treatment experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: H1.2 knock-down triggers a global chromatin decompaction.
source: Concretely, H1.2 knock-down, either alone or combined, triggers a global chromatin decompaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging and DNA-free area quantification in Figure 4.

claim: H1 variants exhibit characteristic distribution patterns in both interphase and mitosis.
source: H1 variants exhibit characteristic distribution patterns in both interphase and mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 1, 2, and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 are enriched at low-GC regions and B compartment in T47D cells.
source: In T47D cells, H1 variants are distributed in two large groups depending on the local GC content. H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 are enriched at low-GC regions and B compartment while H1.4 and H1X are more abundant within high-GC regions and A compartment.
evidence: This is based on previously published ChIP-Seq data referenced in the manuscript (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: H1.4 and H1X are more abundant within high-GC regions and A compartment in T47D cells.
source: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 are enriched at low-GC regions and B compartment while H1.4 and H1X are more abundant within high-GC regions and A compartment.
evidence: This is based on previously published ChIP-Seq data referenced in the manuscript (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 co-localize with compacted DNA.
source: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 are universally enriched at the nuclear periphery in all cell lines analyzed and co-localize with compacted DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing co-localization with DNA in Figure 2.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 showed a coincident pattern with DNA staining, suggesting an enrichment at more condensed-DNA nuclear areas.
source: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 showed a coincident pattern with DNA staining one, suggesting an enrichment at more condensed-DNA nuclear areas, including but not limited to the nuclear periphery (Figure 1A, bottom panels).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images and intensity profiles shown in Figure 1A.

claim: H1.4 profile only partially mimicked DNA pattern.
source: H1.4 profile only partially mimicked DNA pattern while H1X profile was opposite to that of DNA.
evidence: This is observed in the immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A.

claim: H1X profile was opposite to that of DNA.
source: H1.4 profile only partially mimicked DNA pattern while H1X profile was opposite to that of DNA.
evidence: This is observed in the immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A.

claim: Low-GC H1 variants tend to better co-localize with HP1alpha compared to high-GC H1 variants.
source: Accordingly, co-immunostaining of H1 variants with HP1alpha denoted that low-GC H1s tend to better co-localize with this heterochromatin marker compared to high-GC H1 variants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 showed a clear relationship with radiality, becoming increasingly abundant from the nuclear center to the periphery.
source: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 showed a clear relationship with radiality, becoming increasingly abundant from the nuclear center to the periphery.
evidence: This is demonstrated by radial intensity distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: H1.0 was found to be most abundant at the two most peripheral percentiles.
source: Importantly, H1.0 was found to be most abundant at the two most peripheral percentiles.
evidence: This is shown in the radial intensity distribution analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: H1.4 was more equally distributed along A1–A4 sections, being more abundant at intermediate A2–A3 percentiles.
source: A different distribution was observed for H1.4, which was more equally distributed along A1–A4 sections, being more abundant at intermediate A2–A3 percentiles.
evidence: This is shown in the radial intensity distribution analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: H1X was gradually increasing toward the nucleus center.
source: H1X was gradually increasing toward the nucleus center.
evidence: This is shown in the radial intensity distribution analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene-poor chromosomes are located at peripheral positions while gene-rich chromosomes tend to occupy central regions in mammalian cell nuclei.
source: Chromosomes are not randomly positioned in the nucleus; gene-poor chromosomes are located at peripheral positions while gene-rich chromosomes tend to occupy central regions (Boyle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Boyle et al., 2001).

claim: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 were enriched at peripheral chromosomes over central ones.
source: We computed H1 variants ChIP-Seq abundance at chromosomes reported to occupy different radial territories (Figure 1D) and, supporting immunofluorescence quantification, we found that H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 were enriched at peripheral chromosomes over central ones.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: H1.4 and H1X were more abundant at chromosomes located in central positions.
source: On the contrary, H1.4 and H1X were more abundant at chromosomes located in central positions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and to a lesser extent H1.0 were specially detected at the nuclear periphery by super-resolution imaging.
source: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and to a lesser extent H1.0 were specially detected at the nuclear periphery, but SRRF imaging emphasized their presence throughout the entire nucleus, highlighting that these variants are not limited to the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SRRF imaging in Figure 2A.

claim: H1.4 discrete signals were found throughout the whole nucleus, excluding nucleoli.
source: For its part, H1.4 discrete signals were found throughout the whole nucleus, excluding nucleoli.
evidence: This is observed in SRRF imaging in Figure 2A.

claim: Nucleolar H1X was detected but super-resolution accentuated the presence of the non-nucleolar H1X fraction, which was observed throughout the entire nucleus.
source: Conversely, nucleolar H1X was detected but super-resolution accentuated the presence of the non-nucleolar H1X fraction, which was observed throughout the entire nucleus.
evidence: This is observed in SRRF imaging in Figure 2A.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 showed a higher degree of co-localization with DNA compared to H1.4 and H1X by SRRF imaging.
source: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 showed a higher degree of co-localization with DNA compared to H1.4 and H1X, with H1X showing the least co-localization.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2B using SRRF co-localization analysis.

claim: H1X showed the least co-localization with DNA by SRRF imaging.
source: H1.2, H1.3, H1.5, and H1.0 showed a higher degree of co-localization with DNA compared to H1.4 and H1X, with H1X showing the least co-localization.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2B using SRRF co-localization analysis.

claim: Preferential co-localization of H1.0 with H1.2/H1.3/H1.5 over H1.4 and H1X was evident at confocal resolution.
source: Preferential co-localization of H1.0 with H1.2/H1.3/H1.5 over H1.4 and H1X was evident at confocal resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that low-GC variants occupy similar nuclear territories and supporting ChIP-Seq profiling obtained when analyzing T47D cell population.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal co-immunostaining in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: At the super-resolution level all H1 variants co-localized poorly with H1.0, suggesting that they occupy different chromatin fibers.
source: However, at the super-resolution level all H1 variants co-localized poorly with H1.0, suggesting that they occupy different chromatin fibers (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SRRF co-localization analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: H1.0 was anchored to mitotic chromosomes.
source: While H1.0 was anchored to mitotic chromosomes, H1X was not recruited to mitotic chromosomes and it accumulated to the perichromosomal region.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: H1X was not recruited to mitotic chromosomes and it accumulated to the perichromosomal region.
source: While H1.0 was anchored to mitotic chromosomes, H1X was not recruited to mitotic chromosomes and it accumulated to the perichromosomal region.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: H1.3 and H1.5 persisted at mitotic chromatin, being specially enriched at the periphery of condensed chromosomes.
source: Both H1 variants persisted at mitotic chromatin, being specially enriched at the periphery of condensed chromosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: H1.3 and H1.5 layers re-associate with the forming nuclear lamina before mitotic exit.
source: Importantly, H1.3 and H1.5 layers re-associate with the forming nuclear lamina before mitotic exit.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: H1.2 signal was dispersed after prophase.
source: Instead, H1.2 signal was dispersed after prophase (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is observed in immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: H1.2 was re-detected at anaphase, when its peripheral enrichment was re-acquired, parallel to lamina re-assembly.
source: H1.2 was re-detected at anaphase, when its peripheral enrichment was re-acquired, parallel to lamina re-assembly.
evidence: This is observed in immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: H1.2 phosphorylation of Threonine 165 (H1.2-pT165) was found to be highly increased in mitosis compared to interphase.
source: H1.2 phosphorylation of Threonine 165 (H1.2-pT165) and H1.4 phosphorylation of Threonine 146 (H1.4-pT146) were found to be highly increased in mitosis compared to interphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence with phospho-specific antibodies in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: H1.4 phosphorylation of Threonine 146 (H1.4-pT146) was found to be highly increased in mitosis compared to interphase.
source: H1.2 phosphorylation of Threonine 165 (H1.2-pT165) and H1.4 phosphorylation of Threonine 146 (H1.4-pT146) were found to be highly increased in mitosis compared to interphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence with phospho-specific antibodies in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Early-mitotic H1.2pT165 was found to be associated with condensed chromosomes, with maximum levels occurring at metaphase and drastically dropping down at later mitotic phases.
source: Early-mitotic H1.2pT165 was found to be associated with condensed chromosomes, with maximum levels occurring at metaphase and drastically dropping down at later mitotic phases (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: H1.4-pT146 was also more enriched at early mitotic stages, but excluded from metaphasic chromosomes.
source: Furthermore, H1.4-pT146 was also more enriched at early mitotic stages, but excluded from metaphasic chromosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: H1.4-pT146 was accumulated adjacent to chromosomes, in the perichromosomal layer.
source: Instead, H1.4-pT146 was accumulated adjacent to chromosomes, in the perichromosomal layer, similar to what was observed for H1X (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence during mitosis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The peripheral H1 enrichment seen by confocal microscopy for H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 was perfectly resolved by SRRF imaging as an H1 layer adjacent to Lamin A layer.
source: Interestingly, in all three cases, the peripheral H1 enrichment seen by confocal microscopy was perfectly resolved by SRRF imaging as an H1 layer adjacent to Lamin A layer.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: H3K9me2 was found enriched but not limited to nuclear periphery.
source: As expected, H3K9me2 was found enriched but not limited to nuclear periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K9me2 nuclear pattern resembled the distributions of H1.2/H1.3 and H1.5 and a high co-localization was observed at both confocal and SRRF resolutions.
source: Indeed, H3K9me2 nuclear pattern resembled the distributions of H1.2/H1.3 and H1.5 and a high co-localization was observed at both confocal (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and SRRF resolutions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 'Low-GC' H1 variants, including H1.0, were enriched at LADs in comparison to H1.4 and H1X.
source: 'Low-GC' H1 variants, including H1.0, were enriched at LADs in comparison to H1.4 and H1X.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis in LADs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: H1X was located inside nucleoli, with a tendency to form a ring-like layer adjacent to NPM1 on the inner side of nucleoli.
source: Co-immunostaining of H1X and the nucleolar marker Nucleophosmin (NPM1) confirmed that H1X was located inside nucleoli, with a tendency to form a ring-like layer adjacent to NPM1 on the inner side of nucleoli (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 3E, F.

claim: Interphasic H1.2-pT165 was highly enriched within nucleoli.
source: While interphasic H1.2-pT165 was highly enriched within nucleoli, interphasic H1.4-pT146 was not restricted to nucleoli, as it was also detected within the rest of the nucleus, specially coinciding with DNA-free staining regions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figure 3F.

claim: Interphasic H1.4-pT146 was not restricted to nucleoli, as it was also detected within the rest of the nucleus, specially coinciding with DNA-free staining regions.
source: While interphasic H1.2-pT165 was highly enriched within nucleoli, interphasic H1.4-pT146 was not restricted to nucleoli, as it was also detected within the rest of the nucleus, specially coinciding with DNA-free staining regions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figure 3F.

claim: H1.4-pT146 formed clusters of punctate nucleolar staining.
source: H1.4-pT146 formed clusters of punctate nucleolar staining.
evidence: This is observed in immunofluorescence in Figure 3F.

claim: H1.4-pT146 was redistributed to the nucleolar caps upon ActD treatment.
source: H1.4-pT146 was redistributed to the nucleolar caps, as it would be expected from active rRNA transcription machinery components.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ActD treatment experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Nucleolar enrichment of H1.2-pT165 was completely lost upon ActD treatment, and it was not detected at nucleolar caps.
source: Nucleolar enrichment of H1.2-pT165 was completely lost upon ActD treatment, and it was not detected at nucleolar caps.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ActD treatment experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The H1X characteristic nucleolar ring was still found in the remnant nucleoli of a considerable fraction of cells upon ActD treatment.
source: However, the H1X characteristic nucleolar ring was still found in the remnant nucleoli of a considerable fraction of cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ActD treatment experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 'Low-GC' H1 variants were enriched within both NADs and LADs.
source: 'Low-GC' H1 variants were enriched within both NADs and LADs, highlighting their presence within multiple repressive compartments in the nucleus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis in NADs and LADs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 'High-GC' H1 variants are depleted from both NADs and LADs repressive domains, compared to the A compartment.
source: On the contrary, 'high-GC' H1 variants are depleted from both NADs and LADs repressive domains, compared to the A compartment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis in NADs and LADs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: H1X and H1.4 are more abundant at regions that are only classified as NADs (NADs only) than NAD/LAD genomic regions.
source: Still, H1X and H1.4 are more abundant at regions that are only classified as NADs (NADs only) than NAD/LAD genomic regions, contrary to low-GC H1s.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis in NADs and LADs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Multi-H1 knock-down led to a general disruption of chromatin organization compared to control conditions.
source: Multi-H1 knock-downs (KD; i.e. simultaneous depletion of H1.2 and H1.4, see Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017) led to a general disruption of chromatin organization compared to control conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging of DNA in Figure 4A.

claim: Single depletion of H1.2 led to chromatin disruption, albeit to a lesser extent than multi-H1 KD.
source: This disruption was also evident, albeit to a lesser extent, upon single depletion of H1.2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging of DNA in Figure 4A.

claim: Single depletion of H1.4 or H1X did not appear to produce changes in chromatin architecture.
source: In contrast, single depletion of H1.4 or H1X did not appear to produce changes in chromatin architecture at the level studied.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging of DNA in Figure 4A.

claim: The percentage of DNA-free areas was strongly reduced upon multi-H1 KD, supporting DNA decompaction.
source: Thus, the percentage of DNA-free areas was strongly reduced upon multi-H1 KD, supporting DNA decompaction.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4B.

claim: H1.2 depletion led to a decreased percentage of DNA-free areas, although the reduction was minor compared to multi-H1 KD.
source: Similarly, H1.2 depletion also led to a decreased percentage of DNA-free areas, although the reduction was minor compared to multi-H1 KD.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4B.

claim: Depletion of H1.4 or H1X did not lead to significant changes in % DNA-free areas.
source: Depletion of H1.4 or H1X did not lead to significant changes in % DNA-free areas.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4B.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4 were present in all tested cell lines.
source: As previously reported, H1.2 and H1.4 were present in all tested cell lines (Lennox and Cohen, 1983; Meergans et al., 1997; Parseghian and Hamkalo, 2001; Piña and Suau, 1987).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D and supported by cited literature.

claim: H1X was universally expressed in all tested cell lines.
source: Notably, H1X was also universally expressed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: H1.0 was only absent in HeLa cells.
source: While H1.0 was only absent in HeLa cells, H1.3 and/or H1.5 proteins were not expressed in several cell lines, that is Hela, HepG2, HCT-116, HT-29, 293T, SK-MEL-173, IGR-39 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D), and MDA-MB-231 (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: H1.3 and/or H1.5 proteins were not expressed in several cell lines, including Hela, HepG2, HCT-116, HT-29, 293T, SK-MEL-173, IGR-39, and MDA-MB-231.
source: While H1.0 was only absent in HeLa cells, H1.3 and/or H1.5 proteins were not expressed in several cell lines, that is Hela, HepG2, HCT-116, HT-29, 293T, SK-MEL-173, IGR-39 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D), and MDA-MB-231 (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: A simultaneous lack of both H1.3 and H1.5 was consistently found in HCT-116, HT-29, SK-MEL-173, and IGR-39 cell lines.
source: Specifically, we consistently found a simultaneous lack of both H1.3 and H1.5 (i.e. HCT-116, HT-29, SK-MEL-173, and IGR-39).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Cell lines lacking H1.3 and H1.5 tend to have increased H1.0 levels compared to other cell lines tested.
source: Interestingly, cell lines lacking H1.3 and H1.5 tend to have increased H1.0 levels compared to other cell lines tested.
evidence: This is observed in immunoblot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: H1.2 was the most expressed at mRNA level in all cell lines.
source: H1.2 was the most expressed at mRNA level in all cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Simultaneous absence of H1.3 and H1.5 seen at the protein level was also evident at the transcriptional level.
source: Simultaneous absence of H1.3 and H1.5 seen at the protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D) was also evident at the transcriptional level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: H1.0, H1.1, H1.5, and H1.3 expression levels exhibit a negative correlation with gene methylation status in NCBI-60 cell lines panel.
source: Analysis of NCBI-60 cell lines panel showed that H1.0, H1.1, H1.5, and H1.3 expression levels exhibit a negative correlation with gene methylation status and they were not expressed in all cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of public data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: H1.2, H1.4, and H1X genes were unmethylated in the three TCGA datasets analyzed, supporting their universal expression in human cells.
source: H1.2, H1.4, and H1X genes were unmethylated in the three datasets analyzed, supporting their universal expression in human cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In cell lines lacking H1.3+H1.5, a huge mRNA upregulation of these variants occurred upon 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine (aza) treatment.
source: In those cell lines lacking H1.3+H1.5, a huge mRNA upregulation of these variants occurred upon 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine (aza) treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR after aza treatment in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: H1.0 expression was upregulated in HeLa cells upon aza treatment, but to a lesser extent than H1.3 and H1.5.
source: H1.0 expression was also upregulated in HeLa cells (which lack H1.0 protein) but to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR after aza treatment in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: H1.1 expression was upregulated upon aza treatment in all cell lines.
source: Moreover, H1.1 expression was also upregulated upon aza treatment in all cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR after aza treatment in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: H1.2/H1.3/H1.5 were universally enriched at the nuclear periphery in all cell lines tested.
source: Importantly, H1.2/H1.3/H1.5 were universally enriched at the nuclear periphery, as observed in T47D.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: H1.0 and H1.4 were distributed throughout the nucleus in all cell lines tested.
source: H1.0 and H1.4 were distributed throughout the nucleus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: H1X was distributed throughout the entire nucleus, but the intensity of its nucleolar enrichment was variable between cell lines.
source: Lastly, H1X was also distributed throughout the entire nucleus, but the intensity of its nucleolar enrichment was variable between cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Cell lines with a compromised H1 repertoire presented a more peripheral distribution of both H1.4 and H1.0, compared to those cell lines expressing all H1 variants.
source: Indeed, we quantified H1.0 and H1.4 radial distribution (as exemplified in Figure 1B) and confirmed that those cell lines with a compromised H1 repertoire presented a more peripheral distribution of both H1.4 and H1.0, compared to those cell lines expressing all H1 variants (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: H1X was still present at nucleoli in all cell lines tested.
source: Nevertheless, it is essential to note that H1X was still present at nucleoli in all cell lines tested, making it the H1 variant most associated with nucleoli, where other H1 variants are underrepresented.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figure 5D.

claim: H1X showed a strong correlation with %GC content in all cell lines analyzed by ChIP-Seq, being highly enriched at high-GC G-bands.
source: H1X showed a strong correlation with %GC content in all cell lines, being highly enriched at high-GC G-bands (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-Seq analysis in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 5E.

claim: H3K9me2 is considered a conserved chromatin mark of LADs.
source: LADs are enriched in repressive histone modifications, including H3K9me2, which is considered a conserved chromatin mark of LADs (Poleshko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Poleshko et al., 2019).

claim: H3K9me2 plays a part in anchoring chromatin to the nuclear lamina, but it is probably not a sufficient signal in mammals.
source: While H3K9me2 plays a part in anchoring chromatin to the nuclear lamina, current data indicate that it is probably not a sufficient signal in mammals, as other anchoring mechanisms may exist (Harr et al., 2015; Kind et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Harr et al., 2015; Kind et al., 2013).

claim: LADs represent a well-known repressive environment, characterized by low gene density, low gene expression, and a great overlap with B compartment.
source: LADs represent a well-known repressive environment, characterized by low gene density, low gene expression, and a great overlap with B compartment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LADs.

claim: Some LADs have been found to stochastically reshuffled after mitosis and associate with nucleoli.
source: Accordingly, some LADs have been found to stochastically reshuffled after mitosis and associate with nucleoli (Kind et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Kind et al., 2013).

claim: The lamina and nucleolus could act as interchangeable scaffolds for heterochromatin positioning.
source: These observations suggest that the lamina and nucleolus could act as interchangeable scaffolds for heterochromatin positioning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that LADs can associate with nucleoli after mitosis.

claim: A compromised H1 content causes chromatin structural defects in human models.
source: A compromised H1 content causes chromatin structural defects, evidenced both in human (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022) and mice models (Geeven et al., 2015; Willcockson et al., 2021; Yusufova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: A compromised H1 content causes chromatin structural defects in mice models.
source: A compromised H1 content causes chromatin structural defects, evidenced both in human (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022) and mice models (Geeven et al., 2015; Willcockson et al., 2021; Yusufova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Geeven et al., 2015; Willcockson et al., 2021; Yusufova et al., 2021).

claim: Multiple H1 variants depletion leads to chromatin decompaction.
source: Although in these scenarios multiple H1 variants depletion leads to chromatin decompaction, the contribution of individual H1 variants in maintaining chromatin structure has not been studied.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature about H1 depletion effects.

claim: H1 variants distribution in T47D cells was analyzed using ChIP-Seq of endogenous H1.2, H1.3, H1.4, H1.5, H1.0, and H1X.
source: Recently, we performed the first genome-wide analysis of six endogenous H1 variants in human cells, bypassing the everlasting limitation of mapping exogenous proteins (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022 and in preparation for H1.3 data).
evidence: This is stated as work performed by the authors and cited from their previous publication (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: H1 complement is dynamic throughout differentiation and cancer and varies between cell types.
source: H1 complement (i.e. H1 variants and its proportions present in a specific cell) is dynamic throughout differentiation and cancer and also varies between cell types.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about H1 variant expression patterns.

claim: H1.0 accumulates during differentiation.
source: The best-characterized example is H1.0, which accumulates during differentiation (Terme et al., 2011) and whose expression is associated to a less aggressive phenotype of tumoral cells (Torres et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Terme et al., 2011).

claim: H1.0 expression is associated to a less aggressive phenotype of tumoral cells.
source: The best-characterized example is H1.0, which accumulates during differentiation (Terme et al., 2011) and whose expression is associated to a less aggressive phenotype of tumoral cells (Torres et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Torres et al., 2016).

claim: H1.0 has been described as a replacement histone, as it responds to a compromised H1 content.
source: H1.0 has been described as a replacement histone, as it responds to a compromised H1 content.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about H1.0 function.

claim: Combined depletion of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to H1.0 upregulation in breast cancer cells, although without significant redistribution alterations.
source: In breast cancer cells, combined depletion of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to H1.0 upregulation, although without significant redistribution alterations (Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017; Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017; Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: Combined depletion of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to chromatin decompaction at the level of TADs in T47D cells.
source: Moreover, a combined depletion of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to chromatin decompaction at the level of TADs (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022), demonstrating that H1 proteins are involved in maintaining genome structure.
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: H1 proteins are involved in maintaining genome structure.
source: Moreover, a combined depletion of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to chromatin decompaction at the level of TADs (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022), demonstrating that H1 proteins are involved in maintaining genome structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H1 depletion causes chromatin decompaction.

claim: Nucleosomes are grouped in heterogenous nanodomains termed 'clutches'.
source: Emerging evidence from super-resolution microscopy indicates that nucleosomes are grouped in heterogenous nanodomains termed 'clutches' (Ricci et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Ricci et al., 2015).

claim: TADs represent structural chromatin folding units at the sub-megabase scale.
source: Moreover, TADs represent structural chromatin folding units at the sub-megabase scale (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012; Sexton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012; Sexton et al., 2012).

claim: Shifts on the ChIP-Seq H1 variants distribution tend to coincide with TAD borders.
source: In fact, shifts on the ChIP-Seq H1 variants distribution tend to coincide with TAD borders and H1 variants are more homogenous within the same TAD than between TADs (Serna-Pujol et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Serna-Pujol et al., 2021).

claim: H1 variants are more homogenous within the same TAD than between TADs.
source: In fact, shifts on the ChIP-Seq H1 variants distribution tend to coincide with TAD borders and H1 variants are more homogenous within the same TAD than between TADs (Serna-Pujol et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Serna-Pujol et al., 2021).

claim: In single cells, heterochromatic 3D nanodomains tend to be consistently marked by a certain H1 variant.
source: Therefore, a compatible model with our results is that, in single cells, heterochromatic 3D nanodomains tend to be consistently marked by a certain H1 variant.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H1 variants do not co-localize at super-resolution level despite co-localizing at confocal resolution.

claim: Radial position of H1.2-, H1.3-, and H1.5-marked chromatin is inherited through mitosis.
source: These results suggest that radial position of H1.2-, H1.3-, and H1.5-marked chromatin is inherited through mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these variants persist at the periphery of mitotic chromosomes and re-associate with the forming lamina.

claim: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 could be postulated as potential orchestrating factors for chromatin tethering to the lamina.
source: Furthermore, these H1 variants could be postulated as potential orchestrating factors for chromatin tethering to the lamina.
evidence: This is speculated based on their enrichment at LADs and co-localization with H3K9me2.

claim: Lamin B1 KO in human cells led to abnormal segregation of chromosome territories and A/B compartments, as well as global chromatin decompaction.
source: LADs detachment through Lamin B1 KO in human cells led to abnormal segregation of chromosome territories and A/B compartments, as well as global chromatin decompaction (Chang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Chang et al., 2022).

claim: H3K9me2 is reported to safeguard positional information of LADs through mitosis, through a phospho-methyl switch (H3K9me2S10p).
source: This is the case of H3K9me2, which is reported to safeguard positional information of LADs through mitosis, through a phospho-methyl switch (H3K9me2S10p) (Poleshko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Poleshko et al., 2019).

claim: H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 may act as 3D positional 'bookmarks' of LADs.
source: The strong similarities observed for H1.2, H1.3, and H1.5 with H3K9me2 in both interphase and mitosis suggest that these linker histones may also act as 3D positional 'bookmarks' of LADs.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarities in behavior between these H1 variants and H3K9me2 during mitosis.

claim: H1X nucleolar enrichment has been described in previous works.
source: H1X nucleolar enrichment has already been described in previous works (Mayor et al., 2015; Stoldt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Mayor et al., 2015; Stoldt et al., 2007).

claim: Other histone variants have been found at nucleoli, including testis-restricted H1T linker histone.
source: In addition, other histone variants have been found at nucleoli, including testis-restricted H1T linker histone (Tani et al., 2016) or certain core histone variants (Jiang et al., 2021; Long et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Tani et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2021; Long et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2020).

claim: Nucleolar localization of H1X persists after inhibition of RNApol I by ActD.
source: Importantly, nucleolar localization of H1X persists after inhibition of RNApol I by ActD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which was also reported previously (Stoldt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ActD treatment experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and cited from published literature (Stoldt et al., 2007).

claim: H1X might have a more structural role in nucleoli rather than a more functional or regulatory one.
source: These observations might suggest a more structural role of H1X in nucleoli rather than a more functional or regulatory one.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H1X persists in nucleoli after ActD treatment.

claim: H1.2-pT165 and H1.4-pT146 seem to execute a functional role in nucleoli.
source: On the contrary, H1.2-pT165 and H1.4-pT146 seem to execute a functional role, as the nucleolar distribution of these post-translationally modified H1 variants depends on functional nucleoli, with H1.4-pT146 being presumably associated to RNA pol I active transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that their nucleolar distribution changes upon ActD treatment.

claim: The nucleolus is a membraneless organelle formed through liquid–liquid phase separation driven by multivalent interactions of its components.
source: The nucleolus is a membraneless organelle formed through liquid–liquid phase separation driven by multivalent interactions of its components (Lafontaine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Lafontaine et al., 2021).

claim: Nucleolar proteome and specially proteins localized to the nucleolar rim are extremely disordered.
source: Indeed, nucleolar proteome and specially proteins localized to the nucleolar rim are extremely disordered (Stenström et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Stenström et al., 2020).

claim: Histone H1 proteins have a highly disordered structure and have been shown to phase separate in vitro.
source: Histone H1 proteins have a well-known highly disordered structure and have been shown to phase separate in vitro (Gibson et al., 2019; Shakya et al., 2020; Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Gibson et al., 2019; Shakya et al., 2020; Turner et al., 2018).

claim: Almost 1/3 of the candidate H1.0-binding proteins localized to nucleolus and were related to nucleolar functionality in four human cell lines.
source: Proteomic studies in four human cell lines demonstrated that almost 1/3 of the candidate H1.0-binding proteins localized to nucleolus and were related to nucleolar functionality (Kalashnikova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Kalashnikova et al., 2013).

claim: Combined depletion of H1.2 and H1.4 in T47D cells caused a genome-wide gain of chromatin accessibility.
source: This is in agreement with previously generated ATAC-Seq experiments in these cells, which pointed to a genome-wide gain of chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is stated as agreement with previous ATAC-Seq experiments.

claim: Hi-C data analysis in multi-H1 KD cells showed more de-compacted TAD structures.
source: Accordingly, Hi-C data analysis in multi-H1 KD cells also showed more de-compacted TAD structures (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Serna-Pujol et al., 2022).

claim: In mice, multiple H1 variants deficiency has been associated to chromatin decompaction.
source: In mice, multiple H1 variants deficiency has been also associated to chromatin decompaction (Willcockson et al., 2021; Yusufova et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Willcockson et al., 2021; Yusufova et al., 2021).

claim: Both H1.2 and H1.4 proteins contribution to total H1 content is the same in T47D, estimated to be 23–24% in each case.
source: Indeed, both H1.2 and H1.4 proteins contribution to total H1 content is the same in T47D, estimated to be 23–24% in each case (Sancho et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Sancho et al., 2008).

claim: In multi-H1 KD cells, total H1 content is reduced ≈30%.
source: In multi-H1 KD cells, total H1 content is reduced ≈30% and chromatin decompaction is more drastic compared to single H1.2 depletion.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the multi-H1 KD model.

claim: The more drastic effects on decompaction in multi-H1 KD cells seem to be due, at least in part, to the additive depletion of two H1 variants with non-redundant functions.
source: Due to the fact that H1.2 and H1.4 occupy different genomic regions, the more drastic effects on decompaction in multi-H1 KD cells seem to be due, at least in part, to the additive depletion of two H1 variants with non-redundant functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H1.2 and H1.4 have different genomic distributions and their combined depletion has stronger effects than single depletion.

claim: Both the total H1 reduction and the H1 variant repertoire have an impact on the global chromatin compaction homeostasis.
source: Moreover, both the total H1 reduction but also the H1 variant repertoire have an impact on the global chromatin compaction homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of single and combined H1 depletions on chromatin structure.

claim: H1 variants are thought to be specifically distributed among different cell lines based on combining various pieces of evidence from different publications.
source: H1 variants are thought to be specifically distributed among different cell lines, but this presumption comes from combining various pieces of evidence from different publications (Cao et al., 2013; Izzo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Millán-Ariño et al., 2014; Torres et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a presumption based on cited literature (Cao et al., 2013; Izzo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2012; Millán-Ariño et al., 2014; Torres et al., 2016).

claim: No study has properly addressed whether H1 variants are universally distributed or display cell-type-specific patterns up to date.
source: Nevertheless, no study has properly addressed the question up to date.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: The absence of existing reports using standardized experimental and analytical workflows may lead to potential misinterpretation of H1 variant distribution data.
source: Consequently, the absence of existing reports using standardized experimental and analytical workflows may lead to potential misinterpretation of the data.
evidence: This is stated as a concern about the current state of the literature.

claim: H1 variants distribution is conserved among different cell types for certain variants.
source: Our results support H1 variants heterogeneity and suggest that variant-specific functionality can be shared between different cell types.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Compensatory mechanisms between different H1 variants, in terms of distribution, may be limited when perturbing H1 levels but achieved when H1 repertoire is 'naturally' compromised.
source: Our results suggest that compensatory mechanisms between different H1 variants, in terms of distribution, may be limited when perturbing H1 levels but achieved when H1 repertoire is 'naturally' compromised.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H1.0 and H1.4 redistribute in cell lines lacking H1.3 and H1.5, but not in multi-H1 KD cells.

claim: Multi-H1 KD cells are characterized by a robust interferon response, triggered by the expression of repetitive elements.
source: Regarding the functional outcomes of H1-restriction, multi-H1 KD cells are characterized by a robust interferon response, triggered by the expression of repetitive elements (Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017).

claim: Cells lacking H1.3 and H1.5 exhibit a high basal expression of the interferon signature and some repeats.
source: Notably, RT-qPCR experiments indicated that cells lacking H1.3 and H1.5 exhibit a high basal expression of the interferon signature and some repeats (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: H1 variants present a potentially more uniform distribution among cell lines than previously anticipated, particularly for certain variants.
source: Moreover, we showed that H1 variants present a potentially more uniform distribution among cell lines than previously anticipated, particularly for certain variants.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings.
